reason: “out of a rock” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 15:46, and a singleton in a chapter this saturated deserves an answer rather than silence. The temptation is real and it is specifically theological: Mark 15:46 is the burial, a body of flesh laid in a place hewn out of a rock and closed with a stone, and Ether 3 is a chapter about stones worked out of a rock in which the Lord's flesh is seen and a record is sealed up. A reader who finds the singleton will build that reading. The catalogue declines it on the verb. Mark's tomb is hewn — cut away, subtractive, a cavity — and Ether 3:1 and 3:3 both read moulten, which is the opposite operation and is the whole physical point of the verse, since only melting produces stone “white and clear, even as transparent glass”. Strip the verbs and what remains is rock, out of, and the article. Nothing else of Mark 15 is anywhere in the chapter: no burial, no linen, no sepulchre, no rolling. The genuine link at 3:1 is Exodus 34:4, where a man works stone and carries it up a mountain, and Revelation 21:21 for the glass; the Markan echo is an accident of the commonest preposition in English meeting the commonest word for stone.

Not a machine proposal but the association a well-read reader brings, and it needs recording because it survives further into the chapter than most. “white stone” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 2:17, where the overcomer is given a white stone “and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it” — a stone that carries writing only its recipient can read. Ether 3 has sixteen white stones, and twenty-two verses later two stones are sealed up with a text “in a language that they cannot be read”, to be interpreted only by the gift they carry. The convergence of white stone, private writing and privileged reading is striking. It is also assembled from two different places in the chapter, and the wording will not bear it: Ether 3:1's stones are “white and clear”, an optical description of transparency required by their purpose, and they are not the two stones of 3:23, which are never called white. Revelation 2:17's stone bears a name, not a script; nobody interprets it; and the whole point of Ether's stones is that they make another text legible rather than carrying a text themselves. Filed so that a reader who assembles the parallel is told the catalogue assembled it too and declined it. The real Revelation contact in this verse is 21:21's transparent glass, which is catalogued as a link.

A four-word run and the joint top-ranked candidate in the chapter, and it is bare narrative connective. “Went forth unto the mount” differs from “went forth unto the spring of the waters” in everything but the movement verb and two function words. Elisha is healing a water source at Jericho; the brother of Jared is climbing a mountain with molten stones. This entry stands for the whole class of “went forth / go forth unto” matches in Ether 3 — 2 Samuel 13:39 at 3:21 among them — which are not listed individually, per CONVENTIONS §5.

The five-word match is “the earth and the LORD”, which straddles a clause boundary in both verses and is therefore not a phrase at all: in Ezekiel it joins “the LORD hath forsaken the earth” to “and the LORD seeth not”, and in Ether it joins “had fallen to the earth” to “and the Lord said unto him”. Ezekiel 9 is the marking of Jerusalem for slaughter. The real source at 3:7 is Joshua 7:10, whose “Get thee up; wherefore liest thou thus upon thy face?” the machine stream could not see because the Book of Mormon's wording modernises it.

Four words of which three are function words. Genesis 46:29 has Joseph presenting himself to his father at Goshen; the shared string is the reflexive plus the dative plus a conjunction, and it will attach to any sentence in which somebody shows himself to somebody else. The genuine contact for “shewed himself” in this chapter is the post-resurrection idiom of John 21:1, which is catalogued as a link at 3:17 where the phrase is fullest.

The model exclusion for this chapter, because the rarity is genuine and misleading in equal measure. “my sons and my daughters” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 31:28, and “sons and daughters” without the possessives occurs in exactly twenty-six, most of them the begetting formula of Genesis 5 and 11. So the machine correctly reports a five-word singleton — and the singleton is Laban complaining to Jacob that he was not allowed to kiss his grandchildren goodbye. The sense is not merely different but domestic and aggrieved, and nothing else of Genesis 31 is within reach. The verse's real sources are catalogued: John 1:12 supplies the adoption clause, with three separate KJV singletons of its own (“believe on his name”, “power to become”, “become the sons of God”), and 2 Corinthians 6:18 supplies the daughters in the King James Bible's one formula for the pair as divine promise, “ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty”. Note the general lesson: a possessive-plus-plural singleton is almost always an artifact of the possessives, and the count to run is the one without them.

Five function words. Leviticus 5:17 is the guilt offering for an unwitting sin; Ether 3:17 is Moroni excusing the brevity of his abridgement. This entry covers the same class of match at 3:21, where “these things which ye have” pulled Acts 8:24, Deuteronomy 1:18 and John 8:38, and where “the time cometh that” pulled John 16:2. None is listed separately.

A four-word run that exists only in the 1830 text, which is worth stating for its own sake: the first edition reads “the many great works which the Lord had shewed unto him” and the 1920 edition prints “showed”, so the modern text no longer matches the KJV string at all and a search of the current edition would not find this candidate (CONVENTIONS §8). Having said that, the match is not a borrowing. 2 Chronicles 7:10 is the dismissal of the people after the dedication of Solomon's temple, glad for “the goodness that the LORD had shewed unto David”; shew unto is the King James Bible's ordinary construction for divine favour displayed to a person, and Ether uses it four times in this chapter alone (3:13, 3:17, 3:18, 3:26). The real Chronicles-shaped question at 3:18 is not verbal, and the chapter's substantive links stand elsewhere.

sharedText: it came to pass that the Lord
reason: A seven-word run and the longest in the chapter, and it is the Book of Mormon's own most-used sentence opener meeting the King James Bible's. It scored twice, here and at 3:28, on the same string. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5; recorded once here only because the run length will otherwise look like an oversight to anyone reading the dossier. Joshua 1:1 is the commissioning of Joshua after Moses' death and has nothing to do with either verse.

A five-word run of pure donation formula: Jeremiah 45:5 promises Baruch “thy life will I give unto thee for a prey”, which is a rescue from the fall of Jerusalem and shares nothing with Ether 3:23 but the verb and its pronouns. The candidate is superseded rather than merely rejected. The King James Bible has one verse in which God promises to give a man stone — Exodus 24:12, “Come up to me into the mount, and be there: and I will give thee tables of stone”, a singleton — and that is the sentence Ether 3:23 is built on, in a chapter that has been running the Sinai ascent since 3:1. The link is catalogued there.

The best-looking rejected candidate in the chapter, and the one the register exists for. “shewed unto him all” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 4:5 — “And the devil, taking him up into an high mountain, shewed unto him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time” — and Ether 3:25 reads “the Lord shewed unto the brother of Jared all the inhabitants of the earth”. Syntax, verb, spelling, quantifier and the mountain all agree, and the 1830 “shewed” makes the agreement exact where the 1920 “showed” would hide it. It is still the wrong verse, and for a reason a catalogue should be able to state: in Luke the shower is the devil, the showing is the second temptation, the content is dominion offered for worship, and the correct response is refusal. In Ether the shower is the Lord, the showing is the reward of unequalled faith, and the content is not offered but disclosed. A panorama shown from a mountain by a tempter and a panorama shown from a mountain by God are the same stage business in opposite plays. The link at this verse is Deuteronomy 34:1, where “the LORD shewed him all the land” from the top of Pisgah — one of only two KJV verses reading “the LORD shewed him” — which keeps the chapter's Moses frame and gets the agent right.

“And when the Lord had said these words” is the Book of Mormon's standard resumption after reported speech and it appears twice in this chapter, at 3:13 and 3:25. Acts 28:29 is the Jews departing from Paul's lodging in Rome. Covered by the standing formulaic exclusion; the neighbouring 1 Kings 4:34 candidate at the same verse (“of the earth which had”) is a clause-straddling match of the same kind and is not listed separately.
